analogy.p: A recipe says that the ingredients should make 12 cakes: that is the **theoretical yield**. In reality, some mixture sticks to the bowl, a few cakes break coming out of the tin and one is burnt, so you get only 9 cakes: that is the **actual yield**. The percentage yield is 9 ÷ 12 × 100 = 75%. This matches the way product is lost on glassware and filter paper. The analogy breaks down because a baker cannot get more cakes by letting them 'turn back' into batter, whereas in a reversible reaction the products really can change back into reactants.

bullets: **Theoretical yield** = the maximum possible mass of product, calculated from the balanced equation and the masses of reactants.
**Actual yield** = the mass of product actually obtained in the experiment, measured on a balance.
**Percentage yield** compares the two as a percentage, so you can judge how efficient the process was.
Yield is about the **real amount of product made**, not about how fast the reaction goes.
The theoretical yield is a calculation (it needs moles and the equation); the actual yield is a measurement (it needs a balance).
Both yields must be in the **same units** (usually grams) before you divide them.
core.p: The **yield** of a reaction is the mass of useful product you actually obtain. Chemists use two different numbers. The **theoretical yield** is the maximum mass of product that could be made, worked out from the balanced equation, assuming every bit of the limiting reactant turns into product and nothing is lost. The **actual yield** is the mass you really collect and weigh at the end of the experiment. Because real reactions are never perfect, the actual yield is nearly always smaller than the theoretical yield.

bullets: **Percentage yield = (actual yield ÷ theoretical yield) × 100**
Rearranged for actual yield: **actual yield = percentage yield ÷ 100 × theoretical yield**.
Rearranged for theoretical yield: **theoretical yield = actual yield ÷ percentage yield × 100**.
Percentage yield is a **ratio**, so it has **no units** (just %).
Keep the numbers in the same units: if one is in kg and the other in g, convert first.
Give the answer to a sensible number of significant figures, usually the same as the data in the question (often 2 or 3 s.f.).
core.p: The spec gives the idea that the **percentage yield** is the actual yield divided by the theoretical yield, multiplied by 100. Write it down every time before substituting numbers, because examiners award a mark for the correct equation. The result has no units because the grams cancel, so write the answer as a percentage. A value below 100% is expected; the closer to 100%, the more efficient the process was.

bullets: Step 1: **moles = mass ÷ relative formula mass (Mr)** for the reactant you are given (the limiting reactant if there are two).
Step 2: use the **balanced equation** to find the mole ratio between that reactant and the wanted product.
Step 3: **mass of product = moles of product × Mr of product**; this is the theoretical yield.
Step 4: **percentage yield = actual ÷ theoretical × 100**.
Always use the relative atomic masses (Ar) given on the Periodic Table in the exam, for example Mg = 24, O = 16, Ca = 40, C = 12.
Check the answer is sensible: the percentage yield should be between 0% and 100%.
core.h: Calculating the theoretical yield step by step
core.p: You cannot find a percentage yield unless you first know the theoretical yield, and this needs the mole calculation from earlier in the quantitative chemistry topic. The method is always the same four steps: convert the mass of the reactant to moles, use the balanced equation ratio to get moles of product, convert moles of product to mass, and only then compare with the actual yield. Showing each step clearly is the easiest way to pick up method marks even if you slip on arithmetic.

bullets: In a **reversible reaction** the products can react to reform the reactants, shown with the symbol ⇌.
At **equilibrium** the amounts stop changing but both reactions are still going on, so some reactants always remain.
Example: nitrogen + hydrogen ⇌ ammonia in the Haber process only converts part of the gases in each pass through the reactor.
Changing temperature or pressure can move the position of equilibrium, which changes the yield (Higher tier detail in the equilibrium topic).
Answer phrase: **'the reaction is reversible so not all reactants are converted to products'**.
Unreacted gases in the Haber process are recycled to improve the overall amount of ammonia made.
core.p: Many reactions are **reversible**, which means the products can react to turn back into the reactants. In a closed system the forward and reverse reactions eventually happen at the same rate, so the amounts of reactants and products stop changing; this is called **dynamic equilibrium**. At equilibrium some reactant is always left over, so not all the reactant is converted into product and the yield cannot reach 100%. This is one of the reasons the AQA mark scheme expects for why a yield is below 100%.

bullets: **Filtration losses**: some product sticks to the filter paper, funnel or beaker walls.
**Transfer losses**: product is left on the stirring rod, in the beaker or in the flask when pouring.
**Crystallisation losses**: some product stays dissolved in the leftover solution (the filtrate), and washing crystals can dissolve a little more.
**Evaporation losses**: a volatile product can escape as a gas or vapour, especially if heated too strongly.
Spilled or incompletely dried product gives the wrong mass; incomplete drying gives a mass that is too high instead.
Answer phrase: **'some product was lost when it was separated / filtered / transferred'**.
core.h: Reason 2: losses when separating and purifying the product
core.p: Even if a reaction goes to completion, product is usually lost while you collect it. Solid products are separated by **filtration**, and some of the solid is left behind on the filter paper or in the beaker. Transferring a liquid between containers leaves drops behind, and washing and drying crystals can dissolve or crumble a little product. Because the actual yield is the mass of the pure product you end up with, any such loss lowers the percentage yield.

bullets: A **side reaction** is a different reaction happening at the same time that produces unwanted products.
Example: when magnesium burns in air some of it also reacts with nitrogen, so not all of the product is MgO.
By-products must be separated from the wanted product, which can cause more loss.
Side reactions use up reactant, so the theoretical yield (based on only the wanted reaction) is not reached.
Controlling conditions, such as temperature, can reduce side reactions.
Answer phrase: **'some of the reactants react in other (side) reactions to make different products'**.
core.h: Reason 3: side reactions and unwanted by-products
core.p: Sometimes the reactants take part in other reactions at the same time as the one you want. These **side reactions** use up some of the reactants to make different, unwanted products, so less of the wanted product forms. In school practicals the reactants might react with oxygen in the air; in industry, high temperatures often cause extra unwanted products. Either way, the amount of wanted product is lower than the equation predicts.

bullets: **Incomplete reaction**: reaction stopped too soon, so some reactant is left over.
**Impure reactants**: the mass weighed includes substances that do not take part, so there are fewer moles of reactant than calculated.
Poor mixing or too large particle size can slow a reaction so it does not finish in the time allowed.
If you use an excess of one reactant, the other (limiting) reactant controls the theoretical yield.
Measuring errors, such as an inaccurate balance, can also change the apparent yield.
Answer phrase: **'some of the reactants did not react'** or **'the reactants were impure'**.
core.h: Reason 4: incomplete reaction and impure reactants
core.p: If the reaction is not given enough time, not heated enough, or not mixed properly, some of the reactants may remain unreacted even though the reaction is not reversible. Also, reactants are rarely 100% pure: if a sample of 10 g contains impurities, then the real mass of reactant is less than 10 g and the true theoretical yield is smaller than the one you worked out. Both factors reduce the actual yield compared with the calculated value.

bullets: **Percentage yield cannot exceed 100%** for a pure, dry product.
A result above 100% suggests the product contained **water, solvent or other impurities**.
A result close to 100% means the reaction went almost to completion with few losses.
A low percentage yield means high waste and higher cost per kilogram of product.
Compare experiments: the higher percentage yield is the more efficient method.
Be ready to give two different reasons for a yield below 100% (for example reversible reaction and loss during filtering).
core.p: A percentage yield tells you how efficient a preparation was. A high value (over about 90%) means very little was lost, whereas a low value shows large losses or an unfavourable reaction. A yield over 100% is impossible if everything was measured correctly, because you cannot get out more than the equation allows; if it happens, the product is probably impure or still wet, so the mass is too high. Exam questions often ask you to comment on a value or suggest why it is not 100%.

bullets: The **limiting reactant** is the one that is completely used up first and so limits the amount of product.
The **excess reactant** is left over at the end of the reaction.
Calculate theoretical yield from the **limiting** reactant only.
To find which is limiting, convert both masses to moles and compare with the equation ratio.
Using an excess of a cheap reactant can push the reaction to use up a more expensive one.
Unreacted excess does not count as part of the yield of product.
core.p: When two reactants are used and one is in excess, only the **limiting reactant** fully reacts, and the theoretical yield must be calculated from the limiting reactant. If you use the amount of the excess reactant by mistake you will get a theoretical yield that is too large and a percentage yield that is too small. A sensible first step in a longer calculation is to check which reactant runs out first, using moles and the equation ratio.

bullets: High yield = less wasted raw material, so lower cost and fewer resources used.
Low yield may be acceptable if the raw materials are cheap and the product is valuable, or if unreacted material is recycled.
Recycling unreacted reactants raises the **overall** yield of a process.
Reaction conditions (temperature, pressure, catalyst) are chosen as a compromise between yield, rate and cost.
A catalyst speeds up the reaction but does **not** change the equilibrium yield.
Cost and sustainability are the reasons the chemical industry measures yield carefully.
core.p: Companies need high yields because every lost gram of product is wasted raw material, energy and money. A low yield means more reactants must be bought and more waste handled. Chemical engineers choose conditions to give a good yield at a reasonable rate, which is why industrial processes are compromises. For example, the Haber process uses about 450 °C, 200 atmospheres pressure and an iron catalyst, with unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen recycled, because this gives an acceptable yield at an acceptable speed and cost.

bullets: Weigh a clean dry container, add the product, reweigh, and subtract to get the mass of product.
**Dry the product fully**, then reweigh until the mass is constant (heating to constant mass).
Wash crystals with a small amount of cold distilled water to remove soluble impurities with little loss.
Using too much solvent or washing with warm solvent dissolves product and lowers the yield.
Use the **same balance** for all weighings to avoid systematic errors.
Give the actual yield in grams to the number of decimal places the balance allows.
core.p: In a preparation such as making a pure dry salt, you weigh the solid at the end to find the actual yield. To get an accurate value the product must be completely dry and pure, otherwise the mass will be too high. Typical practical points are to weigh the empty container first, to dry the crystals gently in a warm oven or desiccator, and to weigh until the mass stops changing (constant mass), which shows the water has gone. The method also shows where losses can happen, so it links directly to the written questions.

bullets: **Moles and Mr**: needed to find the theoretical yield.
**Conservation of mass**: atoms are not destroyed; missing product ends up in by-products, waste or unreacted reactants.
**Equilibrium (Haber process)**: reversible reactions explain why yield is limited.
**Atom economy**: measures waste in the equation, while percentage yield measures waste in practice.
**Rate of reaction**: affects whether the reaction has finished in the time available.
**Sustainability**: higher yield uses fewer resources, linking to life cycle and resource topics.
core.p: Percentage yield draws together several parts of the chemistry spec, which is why it appears in longer calculation questions. It needs the **mole** calculations and balanced equations from quantitative chemistry, it is explained by **reversible reactions and equilibrium**, and in industry it is considered alongside **atom economy**, rate and cost. It is also tied to the idea of **conservation of mass**: no atoms are lost, but the product that you collect can be less because it is lost, left as other substances, or not fully formed.

bullets: **Percentage yield = actual yield ÷ theoretical yield × 100**.
**Actual yield = percentage yield ÷ 100 × theoretical yield** (use this when asked for the mass obtained).
**Theoretical yield = actual yield × 100 ÷ percentage yield** (use this to find the mass that should have formed).
Both masses must be in the **same unit** (both g or both kg) before dividing.
Use the **formula triangle**: actual yield on top, theoretical yield and (percentage ÷ 100) on the bottom.
Check the answer is sensible: a percentage yield must lie between 0 and 100, and an actual yield must be smaller than the theoretical yield.
Write the unit **g** on any mass and **%** on any percentage yield to protect the final mark.
core.h: Rearranging the equation and using units
core.p: The percentage yield equation can be rearranged to find any one of the three quantities, and exam questions often ask for the actual yield or the theoretical yield instead of the percentage. Because the percentage yield is a ratio of two masses, the units (grams) cancel, so the answer is a pure percentage with no unit other than %. Higher-tier style questions give you the percentage yield and ask you to work backwards, so you must be happy to move the terms around with confidence.

exam: **Command word 'calculate'**: show every step. Typical 3 to 4 mark questions award marks for moles, ratio, theoretical mass, and the final percentage.
Always write the equation **percentage yield = actual yield ÷ theoretical yield × 100** first; this often earns a mark by itself.
For a 4-mark calculation, expect: (1) moles of reactant, (2) moles of product from the ratio, (3) theoretical mass, (4) percentage yield.
**'Suggest why the yield was less than 100%'** (usually 1 to 2 marks): give a specific reason, such as 'product lost on the filter paper' or 'reaction is reversible'.
For 2 marks, give two different reasons, or one reason with an explanation of what it does to the amount of product.
Use the phrase **'not all the reactants were converted into products'** for reversible reactions.
If asked to **compare** two methods, quote both percentage yields and say which is higher and therefore more efficient.
Check your final answer lies between 0 and 100%; if not, you have probably inverted the fraction.
Quote your answer to the same significant figures as the data or to 2 or 3 s.f., and do not round early in the working.
Industrial questions: link a low yield to **wasted raw materials, higher costs and more waste**.
Show units in the working: grams for masses, mol for moles, no unit for percentage.
**Work backwards (3 to 4 marks)**: when given the percentage yield, rearrange to find the actual or theoretical mass, then show each step with units in g.

mistakes.r: Percentage yield = actual yield ÷ theoretical yield × 100; the actual yield goes on top.
mistakes.w: Dividing the theoretical yield by the actual yield.

mistakes.r: Convert to moles, use the equation ratio, then convert back to mass of the product to get the theoretical yield.
mistakes.w: Using the mass of the reactant as the theoretical yield.

mistakes.r: No atoms are lost; say the reaction is reversible, product is lost during separation, side reactions occur, or reactants were impure.
mistakes.w: Saying the yield is below 100% because 'atoms are lost' or 'mass disappears'.

mistakes.r: Give a specific reason such as 'some product was left on the filter paper' or 'some reactants did not react'.
mistakes.w: Answering 'human error' for why yield is less than 100%.

mistakes.r: Use the coefficients in the balanced equation to find the mole ratio.
mistakes.w: Forgetting the balanced equation ratio, for example assuming 1 mol reactant gives 1 mol product.

mistakes.r: A pure dry product cannot exceed 100%; it suggests the product was impure or wet.
mistakes.w: Giving a percentage yield over 100% without comment.

mistakes.r: Percentage yield is a ratio; write only %.
mistakes.w: Adding units such as 'g' to the percentage yield.

mistakes.r: Use the limiting reactant, because it controls how much product can form.
mistakes.w: Using the excess reactant to work out the theoretical yield.

mistakes.r: A catalyst speeds up the rate but does not change the position of equilibrium or the equilibrium yield.
mistakes.w: Saying a catalyst increases the yield of a reversible reaction.

mistakes.r: A percentage yield above 100% means an error, usually a product that is still wet or impure, so check the drying and purity.
mistakes.w: Reporting 105% yield as a very successful experiment.

summary: AQA expects you to calculate the **percentage yield** of a reaction from the actual yield and the theoretical yield, and to explain why the yield of a real reaction is almost always less than 100%. It matters because yield decides how much product a process really makes, which controls cost, waste and whether a method is worth using in industry.

terms.d: The mass of product obtained from a chemical reaction.
The maximum mass of product that could be made, calculated from the balanced equation and the masses of reactants.
The mass of product actually obtained in a reaction.
The actual yield divided by the theoretical yield, multiplied by 100.
The reactant that is completely used up first and so limits the amount of product that can form.
A reactant that is left over after the limiting reactant has been used up.
A reaction in which the products can react to form the original reactants again.
The state of a reversible reaction in a closed system where the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate, so the amounts of reactants and products stay constant.
A different reaction that takes place at the same time as the main reaction and produces unwanted products.
A substance that is made in a reaction in addition to the wanted product.
The sum of the relative atomic masses of all the atoms shown in the formula.
The amount of substance containing 6.02 × 10^23 particles; moles = mass ÷ Mr.
A method of separating an insoluble solid from a liquid using filter paper.
Containing other substances mixed with the substance of interest.
A mass that does not change on repeated heating and weighing, showing that the sample is completely dry.
Separating reactants that did not react and feeding them back into the reaction so they are not wasted.

worked.q: Magnesium burns in oxygen: 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO. 4.8 g of magnesium produces 6.4 g of magnesium oxide. Calculate the percentage yield. (Ar: Mg = 24, O = 16) (4 marks)
steps: From the equation 2 Mg : 2 MgO, so moles of MgO = 0.20 mol.
Mr of MgO = 24 + 16 = 40, so theoretical mass = 0.20 × 40 = 8.0 g.

worked.q: Calcium carbonate decomposes: CaCO3 → CaO + CO2. 25 g of CaCO3 is heated and the percentage yield of CaO is 85%. Calculate the actual mass of CaO produced. (Ar: Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16) (4 marks)
steps: Ratio is 1 : 1, so moles of CaO = 0.25 mol.
Mr of CaO = 40 + 16 = 56, so theoretical mass = 0.25 × 56 = 14.0 g.

worked.ans: Full-mark answer: some product was lost on the filter paper / in transfers (1) and not all the reactants were converted into the product, for example the reaction was reversible or a side reaction happened (1).
worked.q: A student makes crystals of a salt and finds the percentage yield is 62%. Explain two reasons why the yield is less than 100%. (2 marks)
steps: Reason 1: some product was lost when the mixture was filtered or transferred, because crystals stayed on the filter paper or in the beaker.
Reason 2: some of the reactants may have reacted in a side reaction, or the reaction did not go to completion, so less of the wanted product was made.
